paragraphs: Medical vision-language pretraining learns representations from medical images and reports that can support later tasks. Comparing these methods is difficult when studies use different datasets, preprocessing steps, or adaptation procedures. BenchX addresses this evaluation problem by providing a shared framework for comparing methods on public chest X-ray data.

The framework brings together nine datasets covering four medical tasks. It standardizes preprocessing, training and testing splits, and parameter selection. It also provides common fine-tuning procedures that accommodate different pretrained methods for classification, segmentation, and report generation. These controls make comparisons more informative by reducing differences introduced by the surrounding evaluation setup.

The authors establish results for nine existing MedVLP methods using BenchX. They find that improved evaluation and adaptation configurations can allow some earlier methods to outperform newer ones. This finding suggests that reported progress can depend substantially on implementation choices. BenchX therefore contributes both an evaluation resource and evidence that some previous conclusions about relative method quality deserve reconsideration.
neurips-2024-benchx-a-unified-benchmark-.tldr: BenchX standardizes chest X-ray pretraining evaluations and shows that some older methods can outperform newer ones under improved configurations.

paragraphs: Transcriptome foundation models learn from patterns of gene expression across individual cells. The paper argues that treating every cell as an independent sample leaves useful biological structure unused: cell types have established relationships recorded in cell ontology graphs. scCello incorporates those relationships during pretraining to encourage representations that reflect both individual cell types and their broader organization.

The training objective combines masked gene expression prediction with two additional losses. A cell-type coherence loss encourages representations specific to cell types, while an ontology alignment loss teaches relationships between types from the graph. The authors pretrain the model on 22 million cells, using cell-type labels mapped to an established biological ontology.

The reported evaluations cover recognizing novel cell types among unseen cells, predicting cell-type-specific marker genes, and predicting cancer drug responses. scCello shows competitive generalization and transferability relative to existing transcriptome foundation models. The contribution is a way to incorporate structured biological knowledge while retaining a general-purpose model for downstream tasks, including zero-shot use and fine-tuning.
neurips-2024-cell-ontology-guided-transc.tldr: scCello incorporates cell ontology relationships during pretraining to learn biologically structured representations with competitive downstream transfer.

paragraphs: Learning to solve partial differential equations can reduce reliance on expensive numerical simulations, but training these models often requires many simulated solutions. That creates a practical tension: obtaining training data can incur the very cost the learned model is intended to avoid. This paper tackles that problem through unsupervised pretraining for neural operators.

The approach uses unlabeled PDE data without corresponding simulated solutions. It trains neural operators on reconstruction tasks inspired by physics, providing a way to learn useful structure before relying on expensive solution data. The method also introduces similarity-based use of in-context examples to improve performance on data outside the training distribution, without requiring additional training costs or designs.

Evaluations across a diverse collection of PDEs report improved data efficiency and generalization. The method also outperforms conventional models pretrained on vision data in the reported experiments. These findings support pretraining that draws on the structure of the scientific problem itself, together with flexible use of examples, as a practical route to reducing dependence on simulation-heavy training sets.
neurips-2024-data-efficient-operator-lea.tldr: Physics-inspired unsupervised pretraining and similarity-based in-context learning improve neural operators’ data efficiency and generalization.

paragraphs: An agent can learn a control task from recorded data yet remain sensitive to visual changes that do not affect what it should do. DMC-VB evaluates this problem using continuous control tasks with distracting backgrounds, viewpoints, and other visual variations. Its purpose is to test whether learned visual representations support robust policy learning.

The dataset combines locomotion and navigation tasks, static and changing visual distractions, and recordings from policies with different skill levels. It provides paired state and pixel observations, includes hidden-goal tasks, and is an order of magnitude larger than prior datasets discussed by the authors. Three accompanying benchmarks evaluate representation pretraining methods.

The experiments find that pretrained representations do not help policy learning in the main DMC-VB evaluations, with a substantial gap between policies using pixels and those using states. However, when expert data is scarce, pretraining on suboptimal behavior or tasks with stochastic hidden goals can help. These results identify specific conditions where pretraining is useful while exposing persistent difficulty in learning control-relevant visual features.
neurips-2024-dmc-vb-a-benchmark-for-repr.tldr: DMC-VB tests visual robustness in offline control and identifies limited-expert-data settings where representation pretraining can help.

paragraphs: A robot controller that works well in simulation can perform poorly on a physical robot because the simulator behaves differently from reality. EASI addresses this gap by searching for distributions of physical parameters that make simulated state transitions resemble real ones. The aim is to improve the simulator used for transferring learned control policies.

The method combines an evolutionary strategy with an adversarial learning setup. The evolutionary strategy proposes physical parameter distributions, while a neural discriminator evaluates how closely the resulting transitions match reality. The discriminator supplies the fitness signal that guides the search, connecting simulator identification to a learned comparison between simulated and real behavior.

The authors describe EASI as simple, computationally economical, and able to construct realistic simulators with little real-world data. Experiments include both transfer between simulators and transfer to real systems, with superior performance reported against existing approaches. The findings support learning simulator parameter distributions from observed transitions as a useful alternative to relying heavily on domain-specific expertise when choosing simulation variation.
neurips-2024-easi-evolutionary-adversari.tldr: EASI uses an adversarially guided evolutionary search to fit simulator parameter distributions and improve transfer to real robots.

paragraphs: Architectural changes that improve ordinary prediction need not provide the same benefits under adversarial training. This paper investigates that distinction for deep state space models, testing how their structural components affect resistance to deliberately perturbed inputs. The experiments find that pure state space structures struggle to benefit from adversarial training, while adding attention improves the robustness–generalization trade-off.

The authors examine output errors under perturbations through empirical and theoretical analysis. For fixed-parameter models, error bounds depend closely on the model parameters, restricting the benefits of adversarial training. Input-dependent models may instead experience exploding errors. Attention helps by scaling the output error during training, but its complexity also introduces robust overfitting.

Motivated by this explanation, the paper proposes Adaptive Scaling, a simpler mechanism targeting the useful scaling behavior. It achieves adversarial-training performance close to attention-integrated state space models without introducing the reported robust-overfitting problem. The contribution links observed robustness differences to error behavior and uses that connection to design a more focused architectural intervention.
neurips-2024-exploring-adversarial-robus.tldr: Adaptive Scaling helps state space models benefit from adversarial training while avoiding the robust overfitting observed with attention.

paragraphs: Medical image–text models need to learn which visual information corresponds to language. Existing approaches often infer these relationships implicitly from training data, which may limit how well the alignment transfers to other datasets. EGMA introduces radiologists’ eye-gaze recordings as an additional source of guidance for connecting medical visual and textual features.

The gaze data is collected synchronously while radiologists perform diagnostic evaluations. This gives the framework an auxiliary signal tied to the expert’s examination of the image. The approach uses that signal to guide multimodal alignment, bringing an explicit connection to medical reading behavior into the representation-learning process.

The authors evaluate image classification and image–text retrieval across four medical datasets, reporting state-of-the-art performance and stronger generalization between datasets. They also study how performance changes with different quantities of gaze data. Together, these results support the feasibility and usefulness of adding gaze information to medical multimodal learning. The findings concern representation quality and downstream task performance, showing how expert attention can contribute beyond image–text pairings alone.
neurips-2024-eye-gaze-guided-multi-modal.tldr: EGMA uses radiologists’ eye-gaze data to improve medical image–text alignment and generalization across datasets.

paragraphs: Federated offline reinforcement learning asks distributed agents to learn a shared control policy using only their existing datasets. Here, each dataset is small and was produced by a different, unknown behavior policy. The paper observes that simply combining a conventional offline learning method with a conventional federated learning method can produce weak policies.

FEDORA addresses this setting through ensemble learning. It draws together knowledge from the participating clients and distills that collective information into policy learning. The authors also implement the method on a federated learning platform so that it can use distributed computing resources. The central design choice is to explicitly combine client knowledge through an ensemble in this offline setting.

Experiments on complex continuous control environments and real-world datasets report substantial improvements over competing approaches, including offline learning on the pooled data. The paper also demonstrates FEDORA on a physical mobile robot. These findings suggest that how information from different behavior datasets is combined matters: pooling all recordings is not necessarily the strongest approach in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2024-federated-ensemble-directed.tldr: FEDORA combines distributed offline learning through an ensemble and outperforms alternatives, including pooled-data learning, in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Pose-guided person generation aims to create images of a person in specified poses. IMAGPose expands this task beyond using one source image to produce one target image. It supports generating several poses together and using source images from multiple viewpoints, bringing these different user scenarios into a single conditional framework.

Three modules handle complementary parts of the problem. Feature-level conditioning combines texture information from a VAE encoder with higher-level semantic information from an image encoder. Image-level conditioning aligns images with poses, using a variable number of source images and a masking strategy. Cross-view attention separates global and local attention to support detailed appearance and overall consistency when multiple source images are provided.

These components jointly address the need to preserve a person’s appearance while accommodating flexible inputs and outputs. The reported experiments demonstrate consistent and photorealistic generation under challenging scenarios. The paper’s contribution is therefore both a broader formulation of pose-guided generation and a coordinated architecture for retaining detail and consistency across that wider range of conditions.
neurips-2024-imagpose-a-unified-conditio.tldr: IMAGPose unifies multi-pose and multi-view person generation through complementary feature, image, and cross-view conditioning modules.

paragraphs: This paper builds transformer-like networks whose layers correspond to steps of an explicit optimization procedure. The underlying task is interpolation: reconstructing a signal while respecting an interpolation constraint and assumptions about smoothness on a graph. Turning successive optimization steps into network layers gives the architecture a direct interpretation.

The key connection is that a normalized, signal-dependent graph-learning module behaves like a variant of self-attention. Shallow convolutional networks extract compact features for graph nodes, and pairwise Mahalanobis distances define sparse similarity graphs. Given a graph, each layer produces a low-pass filtered signal by minimizing either a quadratic graph Laplacian penalty or a graph total variation penalty.

This construction substantially reduces parameter counts compared with conventional transformers that learn large attention projection matrices. Experiments on two image interpolation applications support the networks’ restoration performance, parameter efficiency, and robustness to covariate shift. The results show how a specified reconstruction objective and learned similarity structure can provide a practical basis for compact, interpretable attention-like processing.
neurips-2024-interpretable-lightweight-t.tldr: Unrolling graph-smoothness optimization produces interpretable transformer-like networks with fewer parameters and strong image interpolation results.

paragraphs: KnowGPT addresses the problem of supplying reliable domain knowledge to language models through prompts. Knowledge graphs offer factual relationships that can ground model responses, but searching them and turning retrieved information into useful prompts can be expensive and laborious. These difficulties are especially relevant when a closed-source model can only be accessed through textual prompts.

The framework divides the work into two parts. A knowledge extraction module selects informative material from the graph. A context-aware prompt construction module then automatically converts that material into prompts for the language model. This design connects information selection with prompt creation, targeting the large search space, API expense, and manual engineering associated with existing graph-enhanced approaches.

The authors report that KnowGPT significantly outperforms its competitors on three benchmarks. Its reported OpenbookQA leaderboard accuracy is 92.6%, described as comparable to human-level performance on that benchmark. These results support the effectiveness of the framework for the evaluated tasks; the human comparison is specific to the reported benchmark performance.
neurips-2024-knowgpt-knowledge-graph-bas.tldr: KnowGPT automatically extracts knowledge-graph information and builds context-aware prompts, achieving strong results across three benchmarks.

paragraphs: Learning diffusion from observations involves recovering the mechanisms governing how a distribution evolves. Existing approaches described in the paper use complicated nested optimization and represent only the system’s drift. JKOnet* aims to make this learning problem simpler while recovering a richer description that includes potential, interaction, and internal energy components.

The method treats diffusion as motion that minimizes energy in the space of probability distributions. It starts from the JKO scheme and uses its first-order optimality conditions to obtain a simple quadratic training loss. For linearly parameterized functionals, the authors also derive a closed-form optimal solution, giving that particular setting a direct route to fitting the model.

The reported comparisons show improvements in sample efficiency, computational complexity, and accuracy. On real-world data describing cellular processes, JKOnet* predicts evolution with state-of-the-art accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost of the existing methods considered. The contribution combines a more expressive account of diffusion with a training formulation that avoids the complexity of earlier architectures.
neurips-2024-learning-diffusion-at-light.tldr: JKOnet* learns multiple energy components of diffusion using a simple quadratic objective, improving efficiency and predictive accuracy.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether mechanisms supporting in-context learning in transformers resemble mechanisms proposed for human episodic memory. It focuses on induction heads, attention components that contribute to learning from the current context. The comparison uses the contextual maintenance and retrieval model, or CMR, as a specific computational account of human memory.

The authors find similarities between induction heads and CMR at behavioral, functional, and mechanistic levels. In language models pretrained on extensive text collections, heads with CMR-like properties often appear in intermediate and later layers. Their behavior qualitatively resembles human memory biases, connecting internal attention patterns with patterns studied in memory research.

The study also removes CMR-like heads to examine their contribution. Those ablations suggest that the heads play a causal role in in-context learning. Together, the analyses establish a computational parallel between transformer processing and a model of episodic memory. The significance lies in identifying a concrete mechanism that can be investigated across both fields, while the reported correspondence remains a similarity between computational systems.
neurips-2024-linking-in-context-learning.tldr: Transformer induction heads resemble a computational model of episodic memory, and ablations suggest a causal contribution to in-context learning.

paragraphs: Learning skills from expert demonstrations does not automatically make those skills adaptable to new conditions or user requirements. LDuS addresses this problem by using language descriptions of a new context to guide a skill diffusion model. Its goal is zero-shot adaptation of a skill-based policy to contexts it has not previously encountered.

The framework uses a language model to generate code defining a loss for the requested context. Iterative refinement checks both the code and the controlled trajectory for alignment with that request in a closed loop. The diffusion process uses this loss for guidance, while sequential in-painting conditions trajectory generation on past state–action sequences through masking.

Experiments on several robotic manipulation tasks evaluate different levels of specification, multimodal contexts, and varied temporal conditions. LDuS demonstrates zero-shot adaptability and outperforms the language-conditioned imitation and planning methods considered. The approach connects a language-level requirement to trajectory generation through an executable objective, allowing the requested context to influence how an acquired skill is expressed at test time.
neurips-2024-llm-based-skill-diffusion-f.tldr: LDuS uses language-model-generated objectives to guide skill diffusion and adapt robotic policies to new contexts at test time.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation addresses learning when the distribution encountered at deployment differs from the source distribution. This paper improves a theoretical framework that measures such differences using f-divergences. Its central contribution is a revised discrepancy measure intended to connect adaptation algorithms more closely with guarantees about their behavior.

The authors refine an existing discrepancy and introduce f-domain discrepancy, abbreviated f-DD. The new formulation removes an absolute value operation and adds a scaling parameter. These changes lead to new bounds on target error and sample complexity, recover earlier KL-based results, and address a gap between algorithms and theory in the previous framework.

The analysis also uses localization to establish a fast-rate generalization bound. Experiments on commonly used unsupervised adaptation benchmarks report better performance for algorithms based on f-DD than for previous approaches. The paper therefore contributes both a theoretical revision and an empirically useful learning criterion: changing how domain discrepancy is measured improves the available analysis and supports stronger results in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2024-on-f-divergence-principled-.tldr: A revised f-divergence discrepancy yields new domain adaptation guarantees and improved performance on standard benchmarks.

paragraphs: In sequential decision-making, the information structure specifies causal dependencies among environmental variables and agents’ actions. Standard reinforcement learning models often impose regular patterns on these dependencies, while some broader models leave them implicit. This paper introduces a model that represents information structure explicitly, accommodating more complex patterns of interaction.

The authors represent that structure with a directed acyclic graph and use a graph-theoretic quantity to characterize statistical complexity. They then construct a learning algorithm and prove an upper bound on its sample requirements in terms of the information structure. This connects the amount of experience needed for learning to the organization of dependencies in the problem.

The analysis recovers known tractability results and offers a systematic way to identify additional classes of sequential problems that can be learned efficiently. Its contribution is a structural perspective on partially observable teams and games: examining which variables depend on which others can reveal useful learning guarantees. The stated bound supplies an achievable sample requirement through the accompanying algorithm.
neurips-2024-on-the-role-of-information-.tldr: An explicit graph model of information structure yields sample-complexity bounds and a way to identify tractable sequential decision problems.

paragraphs: VideoLISA addresses language-instructed video segmentation: identifying the requested object and marking its pixels consistently across frames. Instructions may require reasoning and understanding events over time. Methods designed for individual images face an additional challenge here because they must preserve object identity and segmentation consistency as the video changes.

The model combines a video-capable multimodal language model with the Segment Anything Model. A Sparse Dense Sampling strategy balances information about temporal context with spatial detail under computational constraints. A dedicated tracking token, <TRK>, supports the One-Token-Seg-All approach, enabling segmentation and tracking across multiple frames through a shared token mechanism.

Evaluations across several benchmarks, including the newly introduced ReasonVOS benchmark, report superior performance on tasks involving complex reasoning, temporal understanding, and tracking. VideoLISA also shows promising transfer to image segmentation despite being optimized for video. These findings support combining language-model reasoning with explicit mechanisms for temporal processing and segmentation, and suggest potential for a unified model spanning both image and video instructions.
neurips-2024-one-token-to-seg-them-all-l.tldr: VideoLISA combines language reasoning, video sampling, and a tracking token to segment instructed objects consistently across frames.

paragraphs: Image super-resolution models commonly train on uniformly sampled patches and optimize weights using standard reconstruction losses. This paper argues that such training overlooks imbalances in image content and redundancy in model computation. WBSR reframes super-resolution as an imbalanced distribution transfer problem and provides a framework that can be added without changing the original model structure or training data.

Hierarchical Equalization Sampling addresses the distribution of training examples, helping the model learn from texture-rich content. Balanced Diversity Loss addresses optimization, concentrating learning on textured regions while reducing attention to redundant computation in smooth regions. These components are trained jointly to balance how different image content influences the model.

The framework then uses a gradient projection strategy for dynamic inference. Experiments across different models, datasets, and enlargement factors report comparable or better performance with approximately 34% lower computational cost. The findings support treating training imbalance and inference efficiency together, using the differing demands of textured and smooth image regions to improve the allocation of model effort.
neurips-2024-rethinking-imbalance-in-ima.tldr: WBSR balances super-resolution training and adds dynamic inference, achieving comparable or better quality with about 34% less computation.

paragraphs: Distributed training can spend substantial resources communicating between clients and a server, especially for models with many parameters. Randomized sketching compresses this communication, but earlier theory has offered pessimistic guarantees. Some analyses scale poorly with the full parameter dimension, while others require restrictive assumptions about the information being compressed.

This paper develops a sharper convergence analysis based on the loss Hessian, which describes second-order geometry of the training objective. Using that geometry, the authors obtain guarantees independent of the ambient dimension. Their results also imply communication-complexity bounds that do not depend on that full dimension, providing a more favorable theoretical account of sketch-based distributed learning.

Empirical investigations of the Hessian and the overall accuracy of sketch-based training support the analysis. The contribution helps explain why compressed distributed learning can compete with uncompressed training in practice despite earlier unfavorable bounds. It shows that accounting for the objective’s geometry can yield a more informative assessment of communication requirements than analyses dominated by the model’s ambient size.
neurips-2024-sketching-for-distributed-d.tldr: A Hessian-based analysis gives dimension-independent convergence and communication guarantees for sketch-based distributed learning.

paragraphs: Kernel thinning compresses a dataset into a small representative subset, or coreset, while preserving information useful for statistical tasks. Earlier applications focused on unsupervised problems. This paper extends the approach to supervised kernel regression, asking how carefully constructed compression can reduce computation while retaining useful predictive information.

The authors combine kernel thinning with Nadaraya–Watson regression and kernel ridge regression. For each setting, they show that the compression problem can be expressed through an appropriately chosen kernel, producing kernel-thinned versions of both estimators. The resulting methods provide quadratic speed-ups in training and inference relative to their full-data counterparts.

The theory establishes computational advantages over full-data estimators and statistical advantages over independently subsampling training examples. The paper also introduces a multiplicative error guarantee for kernel thinning and evaluates its design choices using simulations and real data. These results distinguish the two comparisons: compression improves computation relative to using all data, while carefully chosen subsets improve statistical efficiency relative to ordinary random subsampling.
neurips-2024-supervised-kernel-thinning-.tldr: Supervised kernel thinning accelerates two kernel regression methods while offering better statistical efficiency than independent random subsampling.

paragraphs: Adversarial robustness concerns resisting deliberately altered inputs, while membership privacy concerns whether an attacker can identify examples used in training. The paper studies both properties for label-mapping visual prompting, a technique for adapting pretrained vision models. It treats the full reprogrammed system as one model so that the two security properties can be evaluated together.

The motivation is that adversarial training can improve robustness while increasing susceptibility to membership inference. Whether that pattern carries over to visual prompting requires evaluation. The experiments show that the choice of pretrained model strongly affects robustness under white-box attacks, where the attacker has access to model information. Standard adversarial training substantially degrades performance in the studied setting.

By contrast, the transfer adversarial-training approach achieves a favorable balance between transferred robustness and privacy. The authors report this pattern consistently across several pretrained models. The findings demonstrate that security behavior depends on both the pretrained foundation and the adaptation procedure, making joint evaluation valuable for understanding the resulting visual prompting model.
neurips-2024-tarp-vp-towards-evaluation-.tldr: Joint evaluation of label-mapping visual prompting finds that transfer adversarial training offers a favorable robustness–privacy trade-off.

paragraphs: Adaptive learning rates change the size of optimization updates during training, but their long-run behavior can be difficult to analyze. The high line framework studies one-pass stochastic gradient descent on a broad class of high-dimensional problems. It expresses risk and learning-rate trajectories through deterministic ordinary differential equations.

The paper examines idealized exact line search and AdaGrad-Norm in least squares. When the data covariance has strictly positive eigenvalues, exact line search can converge arbitrarily more slowly than SGD using the optimal fixed learning rate. For covariance matrices with only two distinct eigenvalues, the authors exactly characterize the limiting line-search learning rate.

For noiseless targets, the AdaGrad-Norm learning rate converges to a deterministic constant inversely proportional to the covariance’s average eigenvalue. The analysis also identifies a phase transition when the eigenvalue density follows a power law. These results connect adaptive training dynamics to the data’s covariance structure and show, under the stated conditions, that choosing a learning rate adaptively need not improve convergence.
neurips-2024-the-high-line-exact-risk-an.tldr: The high line framework characterizes adaptive SGD dynamics and shows conditions where idealized line search can be arbitrarily slower than an optimal fixed rate.

paragraphs: Neural solvers can perform well on small combinatorial optimization problems yet deteriorate as problem size grows. Dividing a large instance into smaller pieces offers a route to scaling, but existing neural approaches often depend on problem-specific heuristics. They may also train division and solution procedures separately, overlooking how the quality of one affects the other.

UDC introduces a unified divide-and-conquer framework with a Divide-Conquer-Reunion training method designed to eliminate the negative impact of a suboptimal dividing policy. A graph neural network handles division of the global instance, while a fixed-length sub-path solver handles the resulting subproblems. This organization brings the interacting stages into a shared framework.

The authors report superior performance across ten representative large-scale combinatorial optimization problems. That breadth supports the framework’s applicability across multiple problem types and its aim of reducing reliance on specialized heuristics. The central contribution is to treat decomposition and subproblem solution as connected decisions, addressing the weakness of optimizing them through separate training schemes.
neurips-2024-udc-a-unified-neural-divide.tldr: UDC unifies problem division and subproblem solving, delivering strong results across ten large-scale combinatorial optimization problems.

paragraphs: Identifying a causal effect means determining how it can be expressed using observable data; estimating it means computing that quantity from samples. This paper targets the estimation step. Many existing estimators cover sequential back-door adjustment, while broader approaches can become expensive because they require summation over high-dimensional variables.

The authors introduce Unified Covariate Adjustment, or UCA, a class covering a wide range of causal estimands. It includes sequential back-door and front-door adjustment, along with additional expressions involving sums and products. For this class, they develop an estimator whose computation scales polynomially with the number of variables and samples.

The estimator also has a double-robustness property, and simulations verify the framework’s reported scalability and robustness. The contribution is to bring broader causal coverage together with an efficient estimation procedure. This matters because having an identifiable causal quantity alone does not supply a practical method for estimating it: UCA addresses the computational difficulty for the broad class of expressions it represents.
neurips-2024-unified-covariate-adjustmen.tldr: UCA provides a scalable, doubly robust estimator for a broad class of causal quantities, including back-door and front-door adjustments.

paragraphs: When data distributions evolve over time, a model must generalize to future conditions. W-Diff studies a setting where training domains arrive sequentially, rather than being available together. It learns how classifier weights change across domains, using a conditional diffusion model operating directly in the space of model parameters.

The diffusion model receives historical classifier weights as reference points and prototypes summarizing the current domain. It learns the transition from those references to the current classifier’s weights. A shared feature encoder is trained to produce consistent predictions across multiple classifiers, aiming to reduce overfitting and concentrate the learned evolution in the classifier itself.

At inference, the framework cheaply generates many classifiers customized to the target domain and combines their predictions in an ensemble. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report superior generalization to unseen future domains. The method’s central idea is to learn a pattern of parameter evolution from sequential experience, then use generated classifier variation to support robust predictions as the data distribution continues to change.
neurips-2024-weight-diffusion-for-future.tldr: W-Diff learns how classifier weights evolve across sequential domains and generates ensembles that generalize to future distributions.
